lead: The table‑filling algorithm removes redundant states from a deterministic finite automaton (DFA). It works by identifying pairs of states that behave differently for some input. Those pairs are called distinguishable. All other pairs are indistinguishable and can be merged. The result is the smallest DFA that accepts the same language. This minimal machine saves memory in hardware design, reduces software state‑space, and appears in compiler tokenisers and network protocol parsers.
prereq: You need: deterministic finite automata (<a href="#deterministic-finite-automata-dfa">), transition tables (<a href="#transition-diagrams-tables-and-extended-transition-function">).

blocks.text: Create a table that lists every unordered pair of distinct DFA states. If the DFA has n states, the table contains n·(n‑1)/2 entries.
Each entry will be marked if the two states are known to be distinguishable. Unmarked entries are candidates for merging.

items: List all unordered pairs of states.
Mark every pair that contains one accepting state and one non‑accepting state.
Iteratively mark a pair (p,q) if there exists an input symbol a such that the pair of successors (δ(p,a),δ(q,a)) is already marked.
Stop when a full pass makes no new markings.

blocks.text: The algorithm finishes in O(n²·|Σ|) time, where |Σ| is the size of the input alphabet. This bound is acceptable for the small automata used in exam problems.
The first pass marks pairs that differ in acceptance. This step catches the most obvious distinction: an accepting state can never be equivalent to a rejecting state.
After the initial step, look at each unmarked pair (p,q). For each alphabet symbol a, compute the successor pair (δ(p,a),δ(q,a)).
If any successor pair is already marked, then (p,q) must be marked as well because the two states lead to already distinguishable behaviour on the same input.
Repeat the scan until no new markings appear. The remaining unmarked pairs are indistinguishable.

sections.h3: Forming equivalence classes and building the minimized DFA

blocks.text: Collect all unmarked pairs into equivalence classes. Each class represents a set of states that can be merged.
Create a new DFA whose states are these equivalence classes. The start state is the class containing the original start state.
A class is accepting if any member of the class was accepting in the original DFA.
Define the transition function for the new DFA by following the original transition from any representative state and then moving to the class that contains the target state.
The resulting DFA is minimal: no two distinct states are equivalent, and any DFA that accepts the same language must have at least as many states.

examples.question:
Consider the DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) where Q = {q0, q1, q2}, Σ = {0,1}, F = {q0}, and the transition function δ is given by:
δ(q0,0)=q1, δ(q0,1)=q0,
δ(q1,0)=q2, δ(q1,1)=q1,
δ(q2,0)=q2, δ(q2,1)=q0.
Minimise M using the table‑filling algorithm. List the final equivalence classes and draw the minimized DFA.
steps: Mark pairs with one accepting and one rejecting state: (q0,q1) is marked because q0∈F and q1∉F. (q0,q2) is also marked because q0∈F and q2∉F. (q1,q2) remains unmarked.

Check pair (q1,q2). For input 0, δ(q1,0)=q2 and δ(q2,0)=q2, giving the successor pair (q2,q2) which is trivially identical and unmarked. For input 1, δ(q1,1)=q1 and δ(q2,1)=q0, giving the successor pair (q1,q0) which is the same as (q0,q1) and already marked. Hence (q1,q2) becomes marked.
All three pairs are now marked. No unmarked pairs remain, so each original state forms its own equivalence class.
Since no states can be merged, the minimal DFA has the same three states as the original. The transition diagram is unchanged.
examples.answer: The minimized DFA has three states identical to the original DFA; no merging is possible.

traps: Marking only the pairs that differ in acceptance and forgetting to propagate markings through the transition function.
Treating (p,q) and (q,p) as different entries; the table stores unordered pairs only.
Assuming that a pair marked in a later iteration cannot affect earlier unmarked pairs; the algorithm must repeat until no change.
Merging states that belong to different equivalence classes because they appear together in an unmarked pair after an incomplete pass.
Confusing the start state of the minimized DFA with the original start state when the start state belongs to a merged class.

quiz.q: What does a marked entry in the table‑filling algorithm represent?
quiz.a: The two states in that entry are distinguishable and cannot be merged.

quiz.q: Why are pairs consisting of one accepting and one non‑accepting state marked before any other step?
quiz.a: Because acceptance is a property of the language; an accepting state can never be equivalent to a rejecting state.

quiz.q: Given a DFA with states {s0,s1,s2} where s0 is accepting, s1 and s2 are rejecting, and δ(s1,a)=s2, δ(s2,a)=s1, apply one iteration of the propagation step for symbol a.
quiz.a: Initially (s0,s1) and (s0,s2) are marked. For (s1,s2), the successors on a are (s2,s1) which is the same pair, still unmarked, so no new marking occurs in this iteration.

quiz.q: Construct the equivalence classes after the table‑filling algorithm finishes for the DFA in the example question.
quiz.a: All three pairs become marked, so each state forms its own class: {q0}, {q1}, {q2}.

quiz.q: If a DFA has n states and after minimisation the number of states is m, what can be said about the relationship between n and m?
quiz.a: m ≤ n. Equality holds only when no two states are equivalent; otherwise m < n.

quiz.q: Explain how the table‑filling algorithm relates to the Myhill‑Nerode equivalence relation.
quiz.a: Two states are unmarked (equivalent) exactly when they belong to the same Myhill‑Nerode equivalence class for the language recognized by the DFA. The algorithm computes this relation by checking distinguishability for all possible continuation strings.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the table‑filling algorithm in terms of the number of states n and alphabet size |Σ|?

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, minimal DFAs are used to optimise hardware pattern detectors and to shrink lexical analyser tables in compilers. Research extends the table‑filling idea to minimise weighted automata and to handle large alphabets with symbolic techniques. Recent curricula link DFA minimisation to model checking, where state‑space reduction is crucial. To explore further, search for "Hopcroft's algorithm" and "partition refinement" as faster alternatives to the table‑filling method.
